elements.quote: Purpose: This living review aims to critically appraise available data about secondary attack rates from people with asymptomatic, pre-symptomatic and symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection.
elements.reason: The abstract identifies the work as a 'living review', indicating it is a living systematic review of the literature and its aims align with a systematic review.

elements.quote: Purpose: This living review aims to critically appraise available data about secondary attack rates from people with asymptomatic, pre-symptomatic and symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection.
elements.reason: The abstract gives an explicit statement of the main objective/review question.

elements.quote: Study selection: Studies that report on contact tracing of index cases with SARS-CoV-2 infection in either English or Chinese were included.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the main inclusion criteria (contact tracing studies; English or Chinese).

elements.quote: Data sources: Medline, EMBASE, China Academic Journals full-text database (CNKI), and pre-print servers were searched from 30 December 2019 to 3 July 2020 using relevant MESH terms.
elements.reason: The abstract identifies the information sources and reports the date range when the sources were searched.

elements.quote: Data extraction: Two authors independently extracted data and assessed study quality and risk of bias.
elements.reason: The abstract states the methods used to assess study quality and risk of bias (independent assessment by two authors).

elements.quote: Data synthesis: Of 927 studies identi fi ed, 80 were included. Summary secondary attack rate estimates were 1% (95% CI 0% e 2%) with a prediction interval of 0% e 10% for asymptomatic index cases in ten studies, 7% (95% CI 3% e 11%) with a prediction interval of 1% e 40% for pre-symptomatic cases in 11 studies and 6% (95% CI 5% e 8%) with a prediction interval of 5% e 38% for symptomatic index cases in 40 studies.
elements.reason: The abstract reports how results were summarised (summary secondary attack rate estimates with CIs and prediction intervals) indicating the methods used to present and synthesise results.

elements.quote: Of 927 studies identi fi ed, 80 were included.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (80) but does not report the total number of participants/contacts across included studies, so the element is only partially met.

elements.quote: Summary secondary attack rate estimates were 1% (95% CI 0% e 2%) ... for asymptomatic index cases in ten studies, 7% (95% CI 3% e 11%) ... for pre-symptomatic cases in 11 studies and 6% (95% CI 5% e 8%) ... for symptomatic index cases in 40 studies.
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for the main outcomes and specifies the number of studies contributing to each outcome, but does not provide the number of participants/contacts for each outcome.

elements.quote: Summary secondary attack rate estimates were 1% (95% CI 0% e 2%) ... 7% (95% CI 3% e 11%) ... and 6% (95% CI 5% e 8%) ...
elements.reason: A meta-analytic summary estimate with 95% confidence intervals is reported in the abstract, satisfying reporting of summary estimate and interval when meta-analysis was conducted.

elements.quote: Conclusion: Asymptomatic patients can transmit SARS-CoV-2 to others, but our fi ndings indicate that such individuals are responsible for fewer secondary infections than people with symptoms.
elements.reason: The abstract indicates the direction of effect when groups are compared (symptomatic cases generate more secondary infections than asymptomatic cases) and which group is favored.

elements.quote: Transmission Limitations: We excluded some studies because the index case or number of contacts were unclear.
elements.reason: The abstract briefly summarizes an important limitation of the included evidence (exclusion of studies with unclear index case or unclear numbers of contacts).

elements.quote: Conclusion: Asymptomatic patients can transmit SARS-CoV-2 to others, but our fi ndings indicate that such individuals are responsible for fewer secondary infections than people with symptoms.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results and their implications for transmission risk.

elements.quote: Systematic review registration: PROSPERO CRD42020188168.
elements.reason: The abstract provides the register name (PROSPERO) and registration number.

elements.quote: Reports suggest that asymptomatic individuals (those with no symptoms at all throughout infection) with severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) are infectious, but the extent of transmission based on symptom status requires further study.
elements.reason: The abstract states the current knowledge (asymptomatic individuals can be infectious) and explicitly notes an important uncertainty (the extent of transmission by symptom status requires further study).

elements.quote: Purpose: This living review aims to critically appraise available data about secondary attack rates from people with asymptomatic, pre-symptomatic and symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection.

elements.quote: Studies were eligible if they met the inclusion criteria: (a) report on COVID-19 or SARS-CoV-2 infection and (b) report an outbreak investigation or contact tracing study. Exclusion criteria were: (a) review articles; (b) observational studies providing only the proportion of individuals infected; (c) studies that do not indicate the number of contacts or secondary infections; and (d) reports in media sources.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies key study-level eligibility (condition/infection, study design: outbreak investigation or contact tracing) and several exclusion types, but does not comprehensively list all study characteristics (e.g., settings, detailed follow-up requirements) used to determine eligibility.

No explicit eligibility criteria for report characteristics such as dissemination year, language, or publication/report status (beyond exclusion of media reports) are provided in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: A pooled analysis was carried out to generate summary estimates for the secondary attack rate in each subgroup analysed (asymptomatic, pre-symptomatic and symptomatic index cases), in the framework of a random effect model.

elements.quote: Secondary attack rates were computed from raw data in each study, dividing the number of infected contacts of primary cases by the total number of susceptible exposed contacts. A pooled analysis was carried out to generate summary estimates for the secondary attack rate in each subgroup analysed (asymptomatic, pre-symptomatic and symptomatic index cases), in the framework of a random effect model. ... Secondary attack rates are presented as a proportion along with 95% CIs in forest plots.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly specifies the effect measure for the outcome (secondary attack rate), how it was computed (proportion of infected contacts among exposed contacts), that pooled summary estimates were generated using a random effects model, and that results are presented as proportions with 95% CIs.

No thresholds or ranges used to interpret effect size (e.g., what constitutes small/large effect) and no rationale for such thresholds are reported in the provided evidence. The paper reports heterogeneity thresholds (I2 > 75%) but not thresholds for interpreting effect sizes.
No description of methods to re-express synthesized results using another effect measure (for example converting odds ratios to risk ratios) is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The Freeman e Tukey double-arcsine variancestabilizing transformation was used to combine data, because of its advantage over log and logit transformations, which do not allow computation of the proportion in the presence of zero event counts [15].
elements.reason: The authors justify the choice of the Freeman–Tukey variance-stabilizing transformation for pooling proportions (giving a rationale related to zero event counts). However, there is no explicit justification of the broader choice of effect measure (presenting secondary attack rate as a proportion) beyond standard presentation; thus justification is partial.

elements.quote: Of 187 articles retrieved for full-text review and assessed for eligibility, 80 studies were included in the systematic review, and among those we identified 69 studies that indicated the symptom status of index case(s). In this analysis, we excluded 11 studies that reported asymptomatic and symptomatic index cases together or in which no symptom status of the index case was available. We re-classified three studies from asymptomatic to pre-symptomatic as the index cases developed symptoms later during the disease course after reviewing the details and contacting the authors [19–21].
elements.reason: The excerpt explicitly describes how studies were selected for the specific synthesis: number identified that reported symptom status, exclusion of 11 studies that mixed or lacked symptom-status data, and reclassification of three studies after review/contact — i.e., processes used to decide eligibility for the subgroup syntheses.

elements.quote: Secondary attack rates were computed from raw data in each study, dividing the number of infected contacts of primary cases by the total number of susceptible exposed contacts. A pooled analysis was carried out to generate summary estimates for the secondary attack rate in each subgroup analysed (asymptomatic, pre-symptomatic and symptomatic index cases), in the framework of a random effect model. The Freeman e Tukey double-arcsine variancestabilizing transformation was used to combine data, because of its advantage over log and logit transformations, which do not allow computation of the proportion in the presence of zero event counts [15]. Secondary attack rates are presented as a proportion along with 95% CIs in forest plots. Heterogeneity between study estimates was gauged by means of the Cochran's Q and I 2 statistic: an I 2 value above 75% indicates high heterogeneity [16]. Moreover, a 95% prediction interval is displayed in the forest plots, which is an index of dispersion, providing information on how widely the true effect size varies. Analyses were performed though the software METAXL version 5.3 (Ersatz, EpiGear International, Sunrise Beach, QLD, Australia) [18].
elements.reason: The Methods describe how raw data were converted into secondary attack rates, the pooling approach (random-effects model), the specific Freeman-Tukey double-arcsine transformation used to handle proportions including zero events, presentation of 95% CIs and prediction intervals, heterogeneity statistics, and the software used—covering data preparation and conversions for synthesis.

elements.quote: Data were extracted onto a standardized form. elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states that results are summarized in tables and lists the specific data items extracted (author, year, country, sample size, index case details, event details, number of contacts, number of secondary cases), describing the tabular data content.

elements.quote: These fi ndings suggest that individuals who are asymptomatic throughout the disease course are responsible for fewer secondary infections than symptomatic and presymptomatic cases. Most transmission events were associated with living with the index case or group activities such as sharing meals and playing board games. Given the importance of transmission heterogeneity in propagating the pandemic, it is important that we learn about the various factors that contribute to transmission. According to modelling and contact tracing studies, around 80% of secondary infections can be linked to 20% of cases, which distinguishes SARS-CoV-2 from seasonal in fl uenza, although a similar pattern was also observed in SARS-CoV and Middle East respiratory syndrome-CoV [82 e 84]. ... We identi fi ed two other systematic reviews that investigated asymptomatic transmission, with different research questions, which results in different search terms and studies retrieved. One living systematic review, which included studies published up to 10 June 2020, identi fi ed fi ve studies that directly compared secondary attack rates between asymptomatic and symptomatic index cases; all were included in our review [7]. This study only included studies that provided data to allow relative risks to be estimated. The summary risk ratios for asymptomatic versus symptomatic (0.35, 95% CI 0.10 e 1.27) and pre-symptomatic versus symptomatic (0.63, 95% CI 0.18 e 2.26) are consistent with our fi ndings.
